  Much hope was placed on the emergence of biotechnology firms in the 1990s to meet the research and development needs of "orphan" vaccines.  That optimism has been dashed by the reality that such nascent organizations could not manage or sustain vaccine research and development on their own.  Indeed, in recent years many larger biotechnology firms have shed their vaccine business altogether.

  The challenges to the development and introduction of vaccines of importance to developing countries are complex however, and extend beyond market considerations.  In some cases, the science itself is not sufficiently developed to encourage private sector investment in research and development.  Furthermore, the involvement of public sector vaccine institutes in vaccine development is decreasing, and where it does exist, is limited largely to isolated individual initiatives.

  In the last decade, the pharmaceutical industry has seen a series of mergers and acquisitions, with the end result that there are now just 4 multinational vaccine companies in existence worldwide-down from a dozen just a decade ago.  The amalgamation of private vaccine companies has had two important repercussions for the development of vaccines.  First,

  The International Vaccine Institute The International Vaccine Institute was inspired by the Children's Vaccine Initiative, launched at the World Summit for Children in 1990.  The Children's Vaccine Initiative was a broad coalition of multilaterals, public sector, non- governmental organizations, and private industry, brought together to accelerate the research and development of safe, effective, easyto-deliver and widely available vaccines.

  As one of the founders of CVI, the UNDP sponsored a study in 1992 to assess the feasibility of establishing an international institute for vaccine research against diseases prevalent in developing countries.  The feasibility study concluded that an international institute could be effective in vaccine research and development for developing countries, that such an institute could strengthen the capacity of developing country vaccine research and development, and that the most suitable location for such an institute would be in the Asia/Pacific Region.

  Drawing on its comparative advantage in institution and capacity building, the UNDP in 1994 with substantial backing from the Republic of Korea, initiated the process to establish an International Vaccine Institute (IVI) in Seoul, Korea.  The central mission of the IVI is:

  Many of the impediments identified in the continuum of vaccine research and development that led to the establishment of the IVI remain unchanged.  The evaluation team considers the establishment and support of the IVI to be visionary, with great potential to contribute to a greater understanding of disease burden, and the development and introduction of new and improved vaccines.  Investment in vaccines and immunization is an investment in poverty alleviation and sustainable human development.

  With the dynamic changes occurring in all aspects of vaccine delivery, from research, development, management, and production, introduction, and utilisation, the IVI has a clear and unique niche-perhaps more so now than at its inception eight years ago. ### CHAPTER I: INTRODUCTION

##### Introduction and Purpose

Lending is the core activity of commercial banks.  The success of a bank depends on its lending
program and successful lending emanates from well-formulated credit policy.  It is very
important that every commercial bank should have a written credit policy, which should serve
as a guideline covering every major aspect of the lending procedures.

 The primary objective of this Credit Policy is to state the Global IME Bank Limited’s credit
policy and put in place a framework and broad direction for the guidelines, regulations,
procedures and authorities necessary for our entire risk assets business.  This Credit Policy
represents a key element of a uniform, constructive and risk-aware credit culture throughout
the bank.  This Policy seeks to build up a strong credit culture which in turn depends upon
personal integrity of all individuals engaged in marketing, credit assessment, credit approval,
administration, monitoring and recovery.  Building up a strong credit culture also depends on a
commitment of all individuals to discuss issues openly with customers and colleagues and to
place the long term interest of the Bank ahead of the short term interests of a particular business
unit.

 This policy is a guideline to all credit related activities and decisions.  This document is the
principal policy statement of the Bank relating to lending philosophy, culture, criteria,
authority/control, modus operandi and all other issues to bring the uniformity in lending
activities ensuring the best lending practices.

 The objective of this Policy is to assist the relationship and credit personnel to make quality
decisions based on the sound credit principles and procedures adopted by the Bank.

 ##### Short Title, Extent, Commencement and General Guidelines

This Policy will be called the Credit Policy (CP) – Global IME Bank Limited.  This Policy shall
come into force immediately after the approval from the Board.  This CP shall be reviewed at
least once in a year or on requirement basis.

 All the employees of the Bank engaged in any stage of lending operations must at all times be
fully conversant with this CP, its periodic amendments and supplements and ensure consistent
application of the principles and guiding statements laid down here under, ensuring full
compliance.

 The Credit Policy shall be supplemented by Credit Guidelines, Procedural Manuals, Product
Papers, Circulars, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) etc.  as appropriate, approved/issued
by the Board/Management from time to time within the broad framework of this Credit Policy.

inserted, in an effort to make this document as continuously relevant to the changing internal
business dynamics and external environment as possible.

 The version history of such changes shall also be kept on file.

 This policy is strictly an internal document that is intended to communicate, to all the staffs
involved in lending activities of the Bank, the policies and procedures for such activities to
ensure consistent and current guidance to concerned stakeholders.  Any duplication or
communication of this document to unrelated personnel is strictly prohibited.

 ##### Interpretation, Amendment and Review

The Board of Directors of the Bank shall be the final authority to interpret various provisions
contained in this Policy and to approve the amendments or review, as necessary, from time to
time to such provisions.  Any contents not covered by the Policy shall be governed as per
prevailing regulations of NRB and other Laws of the Land.  If any provision contained in this
Policy contradicts with the laws of land, regulatory pronouncements, or requirement of any
internal document enforced/amended subsequent to the approval or revision of this policy, the
provision contained in this policy shall be deemed to have accordingly amended to the extent
of contradiction.

 To supplement this Policy, Credit Guidelines, Product Papers, SOPs and other documents shall
be prepared with detail procedures to guide on proper roles/responsibilities of all the
participants in credit process and implementation of prudent credit practice adhering to the
norms and spirit of Credit Policy.  Credit Guidelines document shall be approved by the Board
and shall be reviewed every year or as and when required.

 ##### Definition

In this Policy, unless the context otherwise requires:

a.  "Bank” means Global IME Bank Limited (GIBL).
 b.  "Policy" means Credit Policy (CP) of GIBL.
 c.  "Board" means the Board of Directors (BOD) of GIBL.
 d.  "Chief Executive Officer" means the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Bank.
 e.  "Borrower or Customer or Client" means person, firm, company or institution

who/which has obtained Credit/facility from GIBL.  It also refers to the
person/institution providing personal/corporate guarantee for such credit.
 f.  “Credit” means, and includes any funded or non-funded amount/facility lent/provided

by GIBL to any of its Borrower or Customer or Client against the security of assets or
against personal/corporate guarantee subject to the repayment of there on principal,
interest or other charge within the certain time limit, direct or indirect guarantee,
interest or other charge of the credit, re-finance, restructuring and renewal of the credit,
guarantee given and other commitment made for the repayment of such credit.

### CHAPTER II: CREDIT PHILOSOPHY AND
 PRINCIPLES

##### Credit Philosophy

Managing credit is one of the most important function in successfully operating banking
business.  While each lending situation is unique, credit officers must evaluate the credit
worthiness of potential borrowers based on most prudent credit philosophy.  Below mentioned
credit philosophies shall be followed by all the credit officers and other participants involved
in credit:

**2.1.1** **Credit Risk Management**

The management of credit risks is approached on three levels:

###### a. The first is on a strategic level where overall credit portfolio of the Bank is maintained

in such a way that no single event can have a significant adverse impact on overall
performance of the Bank.  In addition, resources within the Bank are deployed so as to
take maximum advantage of profitable credit risk opportunities in its target markets i.e.
 to maintain business expansion assuming acceptable credit risk.
 ###### b. On a second level, the Bank establishes credit policies and procedures which provide a

minimum standard for credit activities and foster a common approach to credit risk
management by individual relationship units / branches.  These are established to
provide a prudent framework for individual credit / relationship officers to operate
within.
 ###### c. On a third level, the Bank relies on the competence of the staff involved in credit related

activities to identify acceptable credit risks and to make sound decisions in the approval
and ongoing management of those risks.

 **2.1.2** **Acceptable Credit Risks**

a. Responsibility for defining the characteristics of acceptable credit risks is given to

individual Business Units and Branches who exercise their judgment guided by the
Bank’s strategy and objectives.  This involves:

i. Identifying appropriate target markets.
 ii.  Establishing the characteristics of desirable customers within identified target
markets.
 iii.  Assessing whether adequate resources are available to properly manage
acceptable risk assets.
 iv.  Ensuring that economic, cultural, and regulatory requirements of the country are
respected.
 v. Ensuring the portfolio of assets is consistent with the Bank’s strategy and
objectives, particularly in relation to risk concentrations, maturity profiles and
liquidity management.

important centers of responsibility in the credit risk management process which will be

 c. To enable each of these centers to achieve their individual objectives, the Bank

distinguishes between the credit risk approval process and the credit proposal writing
process.  In short, the credit risk approval process determines the safety of an exposure
whilst the credit proposal writing process is the undertaking of an exposure by a
Business Unit / Branch which is compatible with its business objectives.
 d. A suitable balance between risk and reward from the Bank’s perspective is achieved by

relying on the judgment of individual officials as well as the use of tiered levels of
responsibility to satisfy the requirement of both the credit approval process and the
credit proposal writing process.

 **2.1.3** **Use of Common Sense**

An important factor determining the quality of the Bank’s credit risk assets is the caliber of the
decisions of staff involved in the credit process.  Considerable reliance is placed on the use of
common sense and past experience in conjunction with thorough evaluations and credit
analysis.

 Credit assessment will include the application of certain observations or principles.  The most
basic of these are:

a. Repayment is dependent on the customer generating cash and applying it to liquidate

exposures.  Credit assessment must accordingly look to the customer’s capacity and
willingness to repay.
 b. The quality of credit assessment depends on the quality of analysis undertaken and the

reliability of the data used.  Basing credit decisions solely on the basis of reputation,
accepted practice, other lenders’ credit risk assessment or the recommendations of other
officers is not prudent behavior.
 c. Rational credit assessment involves assessing the probabilities and consequences of the

“worst case”.  This includes evaluating cash flows, balance sheet items and security on
both a “going concern” and a “distressed sale” basis.
 d. The value of security does not guarantee the safety of an exposure.  Security is a “second

way out” and exposure should not be undertaken where the safety is justified only on
the basis of the value of security held.
 e. Any security taken to offset weakness in ability to honor obligations when they fall due

must be readily realizable.
 f. It is prudent to take available additional security even though the credit assessment may

indicate that the credit risks are acceptable even with existing/proposed securities.

 ##### Credit Principles:

Credit analysis is a method by which Bank ascertains the credit worthiness of a business or
organization.  Fundamental Five “C’s” of credit analysis includes Character, Capacity, Capital,
Collateral and Conditions which should be borne in mind while lending credit facilities to the
Borrower.  These five characteristics of the Borrower incorporate both qualitative and
quantitative measures.

 The first factor is 'Character', which refers to a borrower's reputation.  'Capacity' measures a
borrower's ability to repay a loan by comparing income against obligation.  The lender will
consider any 'Capital' the borrower puts toward a potential investment, because a large
contribution by the borrower will lessen the chance of default.  'Collateral', which is easily
salable/marketable, helps to secure the loan.  Finally, the 'Conditions' of the loan, such as the
interest rate and amount of principal, will influence the lender's desire to finance the borrower.

 Credit policies and procedures can never capture all the complexities of Bank’s business.
 Therefore, the following Credit Principles are the ultimate reference point for all Bank staff
when making lending decisions:

a. Understand the need of the customer
b. Understand the borrower, business and the related risks.

### CHAPTER III: CREDIT MANAGEMENT AND

##### Credit Management Process

Bank shall have online credit workflow system constituting all steps for credit approval and
disbursal.  Credit Management process generally involves the phases as briefly explained herein
under:

**3.1.1** **Pre-Approval**

Pre-approval involves the activities undertaken prior to approval/sanction of credit facilities.
 The key activities under this phase include marketing & solicitation, application /document
collection, initial screening of credit requests from branches/units.

 **3.1.2** **Approval Process**

Approval process is initiated by branches/units with preparation of detailed Credit Proposal
with detailed credit analysis, risk rating and approve as per the delegated credit authority, if
any or recommend the same to appropriate approval/review chain for needful
evaluation/approval.  Proposal received with branch/unit recommendation are then duly
reviewed/evaluated by all the concerned under the approval chain who shall either approve or
reject the proposal based on their analysis.

 **3.1.3** **Implementation**

Implementation process is initiated upon approval/sanction of the credit request.  The key
activities under this phase include issuance of offer letter as the notification of the approved
facilities and the applicable terms, execution of documents followed by
implementation/disbursement of credit facilities as per the approved terms and conditions.

### CHAPTER IV: CREDIT LIMITS & FACILITIES

##### Credit Limit

"Credit Limit" is a figure used as part of the Bank’s credit control system to reflect the Bank’s
approved exposure to counterparty.  Credit limits are required to be in place when the Bank
assumes credit risk for approved party.

 Credit limits may be revolving or terminating.  Terminating limits are the limits which are
repayable in several installments or in one installment after a period of time and which cannot
be redrawn once they have been utilized or repaid.  Revolving limits are the limits, which are
available until cancelled, and subject to periodic or annual review.  Borrowers can borrow,
repay and re-borrow the revolving limits.  Bank may also provide foreign currency credit limit
in line with NRB directives.

 ##### Tenor of Loan

Risk increases with the increases in the tenor of credit limits as there is uncertainty and
unpredictable environment due to regulatory changes, economic trends/ cycle, borrower
specific industry.  Hence, tenor of the Loan shall be decided based on cash flow projection
and/or business requirements of the client, or as mentioned in the respective product paper or
other policy/guidelines.

 ##### Types of Credit Facilities

**4.3.1** **Funded Facilities**

Funded facilities refer to the credit facilities where the funds are disbursed.  The funded
facilities shall be further classified as under:

**4.3.1.1** **Working Capital Loans**
Working capital loan is extended to fulfill the borrower’s working capital requirement and is
generally provided as follows.  Working capital loan is regulated by the drawing power of the
borrower, which represents the allowable Debt Equity (D/E) Ratio on their Net Trading Assets/
Net Working Capital Requirement.

 The key credit products under this category are as follows:

a.  **Overdraft:**

Overdraft facility is a kind of working capital loan.  It is a running loan account and
shall be operated by cheques on a current account.  The borrower shall be allowed to
overdraw his/her current account within prescribed limit and for stipulated time period.
 The borrower can deposit any amount in this account.  Thus, the balance will be
fluctuating due to withdrawal and repayment of money by the borrower.  Overdraft will
generally be granted for the fulfillment of borrowers’ short-term credit needs.

paying the Bank on TR due date.

requirement.  Export credit is generally classified into following two categories on the
basis of stage of the export:

i.  **Pre-Shipment Credit: Pre-shipment credits are usually provided to the exporters**
to purchase the raw material required for production and export of the goods.  Preshipment credit will be granted on the basis of a confirmed letter of credit or
against a purchase order and are usually liquidated by negotiating bills or by the
post-shipment credit.

 ii.  **Post-Shipment Credit: The Bank will extend post-shipment credit through**
purchase/discount of export bills or by way of advance against such bills.  The

Term Loan refers to the loans that have a specified repayment schedule.  Such loans are

### CHAPTER V: SINGLE OBLIGOR AND RISK
 DIVERSIFICATION

##### Grouping of Customers 

Considering that the banks and financial institution (BFIs) use depositors’ money for lending,
none of bank can be exposed to a single group of borrowers beyond its comfort level in relation
to its core capital/total capital.  So it is of utmost necessity for the Bank to have procedures to
identify situations where, in considering credits, it is appropriate to classify a group of obligors
as connected counterparties and, thus, as a single obligor.  This would include aggregating
exposures to groups of accounts exhibiting financial interdependence, including corporate or
non-corporate, where they are under common ownership or control or with strong connecting
links.  Bank need to develop and implement comprehensive procedures and information
systems to monitor the condition of individual credits and single obligors across the bank’s
various portfolios.  Bank also need to follow Nepal Rastra Bank provisions regarding grouping
of borrowers.

 ##### Single Obligor Limit

Single obligor limit refers to the credit exposure to the group of borrowers.  As cited above, to
ensure that the Bank is not significantly affected with the non-functioning of any particular
obligor group of risk assets, bank needs to set an internal threshold limit in relation to its core
capital/total capital that it can extend to a Single Obligor Group.  While setting the single
obligor limit, Bank also need to follow NRB provisions on same.  Exposure to the obligor group
should be assessed and considered on each credit approval / disbursement.

 ##### Risk Diversification

a. The Bank shall diversify its risk portfolio in order to reduce concentration risk, such

that the stakes of the Bank, in the eventuality of one customer having in default or one
sector of the economy gets into trouble, does not get threatened and Bank's balance
sheet is managed prudently.
 b. For the purpose of prudent banking practice, the Bank shall diversify its risk asset

portfolio among several sectors and sub sectors of the economy over a large number of
customers as far as possible.
 c. Bank shall at all times adhere to the Single Obligor Limit (SOL) and Sectoral Cap /

portfolio Cap requirement prescribed by Nepal Rastra Bank for a Customer or
Customer Group.
 d. The management, if required, may prescribe internal SOL and Sectoral Cap for the

better management of sectoral concentration and prudential lending limit.

### CHAPTER VI: RISK GRADING

##### Know Your Customer (KYC)

The loan shall be extended to such customers only whose proper information in terms of
general, financial etc.  have been obtained and assessed properly.  The principle “Know Your
Customer” applies in every circumstance and in every line of business in which the Bank is
engaged.  Borrower KYC is crucial for assessment of repayment capacity, repayment
willingness of the borrower, social standing, involvement in other business, etc.  Here bank
shall not only limit to the information provided by the borrower but also explore additional
information from various other sources available like social media, relationship with
buyer/supplier, credit behavior etc.

 The Bank shall not pursue or maintain relationship with customers from whom all information
required as a part of “Know Your Customer” cannot be obtained.  The Bank shall cautiously
check the background of the customer through laid down process and procedures of the Bank
through internal and external databases so as to confirm the adherence/compliance of the Bank
towards Anti Money Laundering (AML) and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT).  In
this regard, Bank’s internal policy and guidelines on AML/KYC/CFT also to be followed.
 These review shall also help in Risk Grading/Rating of customers.

 ##### Borrower's Risk Grading/Rating

Risk grading/rating of the customers or portfolio shall be done based on separate guidelines
formulated by the Management.  Such grading system to be developed based on best national
and international practices covering various factors so that credit officers are able to make
various decisions including approval/ rejection, pricing, security and other terms / covenants
applicable for each credit relationship based on such grading/rating.

 Under such guidelines, management must also include provisions regarding appropriate action
to be taken in case of downgrading of any customer.  Further, improvement in grade alone shall
not necessarily lead to increase in current exposure of any customer.

 ##### Management Information System (MIS)

Each credit proposal (normally repeat clients) should contain history of borrower so that credit
officers including branches/province is able to review position of customer at a glance.  Such
history need to be supported by a proper Management Information System (MIS) and such data
shall facilitate in generating risk grading/rating of any customer.  The management shall, on a
continuous basis, develop and circulate various MIS formats as required.  Management may
assign various technical units/department for development of various reports under MIS which
shall support the decision making process of Branch, Province and various Credit Officers.

### CHAPTER VII: ENVIRONMENT AND SOCIAL RISK
 MANAGEMENT

Environmental risks pertain to the potential for damage of the environment and ecosystem.  The
principal sources of such potential damage are pollution of the air, water and land resulting
from industrial activity.  Environmental risks are largely a function of the nature (i.e.  sector) of
the business activity.  Social risks pertain to the potential of business activities to cause an
adverse impact such as damage, injury or loss to persons (e.g.  employees, customers) and
communities (e.g.  neighbors).  Social risks are largely a function of the client’s behavior.

 The Bank is exposed to some level of E&S risk through their clients.  If left unmanaged, these
risks can lead to a decline in the Bank’s reputation, costly litigation, or loss of revenue.  The
type, quantity and severity of Environment and Social (E&S) issues that present a risk to the
Bank for any given transaction depend on a variety of factors, including geographic context,
industry sector, scale of the activity, and the type of transaction (e.g.  SME finance, Term
Finance, project finance, commercial leasing).

 Hence, a proper Environmental & Social Risk Management (ESMS) should be in place that
helps the Bank to reduce the transaction risks resulting from E&S risk factors associated with
their clients’ business activities.  A separate policy and guidelines relating to E&S Risk
management should be in place so as to integrate the E&S Risk Management process in existing
overall credit risk management process.

### CHAPTER VIII: CREDIT APPROVAL DISCRETIONS

##### Credit Officers

“Credit Officers” means the **employees who have been entrusted with the authority to**
**recommend/approve/reject the credit facilities.  Such officers can be broadly classified into**
different classes on the basis of corporate position they hold.  Class category of credit officers
shall be defined in Credit Guidelines.

 ##### Approval Authority Matrix

The approval authority refers to limit that any credit officer is entrusted with to approve to any
customer or group.  Approval Authority for various Credit Officers shall be as approved by the
CEO remaining within the credit officers’ class wise approval authority matrix as provided in
Credit Guidelines.  Credit Approval Authority matrix shall provide the highest approving
authority limit that the CEO can delegate to different classes of credit officers.

 ##### Delegation of Credit Approval Discretion (CAD)

a. The BOD is the ultimate / highest approving authority of the bank.
 b. BOD shall delegate the lending authority to the Chief Executive Officer.
 c. CEO may re-delegate CAD delegated to him/her by the BOD to various credit officers,

based on the approval authority matrix guidelines.
 d. Credit Officers should not automatically get approving authority by virtue of his / her

corporate and / or functional title.  Such authority shall not be delegated to a position
but to the incumbent as per approving authority matrix.  The credit approval authority
assigned to individual credit officer shall be valid till the incumbent holds the position
for which the same has been assigned.  Lending authority shall cease automatically once
the officer is transferred from that position.  CEO has the right to change, within the
credit authority matrix, or cancel the approval authority assigned to any credit officer
as deemed necessary.
 e. Credit/facility may only be approved within the authority levels of formally delegated

Credit Approval Discretions.
 f. Credit authority is delegated based on individual experience, job role, qualification and

proven capacity.  Hence, credit officers holding same corporate designation or within
the same Class may be assigned with different credit authority limit based on their
experience, job role, education qualification, annual performance review and proven
capacity.
 g. Credit Approving Authority of each credit officer may change during review of

authority delegation based on his/her performance, proven capacity and other
indicators.
 h. Credit officer shall remain responsible and accountable while exercising credit

authority delegated to him/her.

**recommend/approve/reject the credit facilities.  Such officers can be broadly classified into**
different classes on the basis of corporate position they hold.  Class category of credit officers
shall be defined in Credit Guidelines.

 ##### Approval Authority Matrix

The approval authority refers to limit that any credit officer is entrusted with to approve to any
customer or group.  Approval Authority for various Credit Officers shall be as approved by the
CEO remaining within the credit officers’ class wise approval authority matrix as provided in
Credit Guidelines.  Credit Approval Authority matrix shall provide the highest approving
authority limit that the CEO can delegate to different classes of credit officers.

 ##### Delegation of Credit Approval Discretion (CAD)

a. The BOD is the ultimate / highest approving authority of the bank.
 b. BOD shall delegate the lending authority to the Chief Executive Officer.
 c. CEO may re-delegate CAD delegated to him/her by the BOD to various credit officers,

based on the approval authority matrix guidelines.
 d. Credit Officers should not automatically get approving authority by virtue of his / her

corporate and / or functional title.

### CHAPTER IX: CREDIT PROPOSAL

"Credit Proposal" is the term given to a collection of documents, submission of required
information under a stated format, credit assessment, credit review and approval; which
formally record the basis on which the Bank undertakes/ underwrites credit risk.

 A credit proposal is required whenever it is necessary to formally record the basis on which the
Bank assumes credit risk.  The credit proposal should clearly demonstrate why the exposure
does (or does not) represent an acceptable risk.

 The comments of a supporting and approving officers form integral part of the credit proposal.

 The exact format for various types of credit limits / customers will be as approved by the Chief
Executive Officer his/her designated alternate from time to time.  This Format could be in the
**Digital Form as well.  Any omission of any part of the proposal shall not be allowed,** **even**
**though they may not be relevant for the specific case. **

The Bank may design various templates of Credit Proposal formats for various business
segments based on the size of exposure, credit facility complexities etc.  Credit proposals shall
be processed via a proper system where digitization to be prioritized to the possible extent.
 **Such formats/template may differ in the case of Digitized process, however, it should be**
**approved by CEO or authority delegated by him/her. **

### CHAPTER X: COLLATERAL/SECURITIES AND
 SECURITY DOCUMENTATION

##### General

The value of security held does not guarantee the safety of an exposure.  The securities are
“Second Way Out” in distressed situation and exposure should not be undertaken where the
safety is justified only on the basis of the value of security held unless the security is liquid
cash collateral or cash equivalent collateral.  Primary source for the repayment of debt is the
income of business or the cash generated from the business.

 The bank shall have basically following three layers of security, depending upon the nature of
credit product of facility:

a.  **Primary Security:**

The bank shall have charge over the asset or project that has been financed, through
appropriate procedure.  For the assets that require registration in the government or other
related agencies / offices to create the charge, the same shall be executed.  However, for
the assets that do not have such provision, the charge shall be created through
appropriate internal documentation, as per the Banks internal policies, NRB directives
or the land of the law.

 b.  **Secondary Security:**

The bank may seek for the securities other than primary security as required by the
specific product paper, nature of primary security or the terms of approval, as deemed
necessary.  Charge over such assets shall be created, as required.

 c.  **Additional Security:**

The security obtained for additional comfort above the primary and secondary security
shall serve as additional security.

 Bank shall always seek to obtain various additional forms of securities deemed necessary to
safeguard any Credit extended to any borrower which may even be a third party security.
 Third party security refers to those collaterals as per third party definition laid down by NRB
Unified Directives.  General policy of the Bank is not to accept third party security.  However,
in exceptional situations where obtaining of third party collateral is beneficial to the Bank
(such as during recovery of loans), such collateral may be accepted upon approval from the
CEO or other Credit Officers as delegated by CEO.

##### Types of Securities and Security Coverage Requirement

Types of securities and security coverage requirement for various types of credit products and
customers shall be standardized in respective Credit Guideline or in Product Paper Guideline.

 ##### Valuation of Securities

Valuation/revaluation of real estate property and fixed assets (to be) mortgaged with the Bank
must be carried out by professional valuator of the Bank as mentioned in respective Product
Paper Guideline, Credit Guidelines or Valuation Guideline of the Bank.  However, exception
on valuation by listed valuator can be provided for specific loan based on size/type and as
allowed by NRB or Product Paper of the Bank.

 The Bank shall have separate Valuation Guideline for guiding Selection/ appointment/ review/
renewal/ delisting process of authorized valuator of the Bank, agreement between Bank and
Valuator, valuation criteria for valuation of property/assets, valuation cap to various valuators,
etc.

 ##### Security Documentation

In order to be recognized as security, all items hypothecated/mortgaged/pledged must have
value and/or legal title thereto, together with the necessary documentation to enable us to
realize the assets without the requirement of co-operation of the security owner.

 In general, security documents are the documents having financial values which are executed
by customers in the Bank’s and/or regulators prescribed formats which strengthens the bank’s
position to recover the loans and advances extended to the customers in case the customer
defaults.  Standard security documents as approved by the CEO with notification to BOD must
always be used.  Any deviation would require legal opinion from legal department of the bank
and approval of the Chief Executive Officer or his/her designated alternate.

 The procedures for development of security documentations shall be as follows:

a. Legal Department shall prepare the format of security documentation considering

requirement of Credit Administration Department (CAD).
 b. CAD shall forward security documentation format to Business Unit and Integrated Risk

Management Department for review and support.
 c. The Documents shall also be reviewed and vetted by legal advisor.
 d. The security documentation format should be forwarded for approval from CEO or

his/her designated alternate with subsequent notification to the Board.

### CHAPTER XI: RETURN AND PRICING

Pricing is generally determined in accordance with the goal to optimize earnings taking into
consideration the various factors such as cost of funds, return on capital employed, Base rate,
tax implications, if any, administrative expenses, extent of risk, total amount of banking
business placed by the customer with the Bank, competitive conditions, and restrictions, if any,
placed by regulators or prevailing laws.

 Asset Liability Management Committee (ALCO) is the final authority to decide on the interest
rates structure of all the loan products/services.  Furthermore, ALCO shall review/study the
interest rates periodically on need basis and make necessary changes/amendment therein from
time to time so as to be compatible with the market and also for ensuring a reasonable
spread/income.

 The Bank shall price the credit transaction based on inherent risks with the transaction,
availability of risk mitigants, market behaviour/sentiments etc.  ensuring that all credit
extensions shall be profitable transactions which shall be reviewed from computed Return on
Regulatory Capital.

 The Bank will have schedule of fees and charges and interest rates of the Bank.  These are to
be periodically amended and made available to the general public as per regulations of the
Nepal Rastra Bank.

 The Bank shall comply with all the pricing related directives of the Nepal Rastra Bank.

 Loan administration fees, commitment fees, prepayment fees, late payment fees as allowed by
NRB, Commission and charges associated with both the funded and non-funded loan
products/services will be levied as per the Schedule of Fees and Charges (SFC) of the Bank
which shall also be decided, changed/amended and approved by the ALCO from time to time.

 Any exception or downward deviation from published interest rates as well as Schedule of Fees
and Charges of the Bank while charging the interest/fees/commission to loan clients must be
approved/authorized by CEO or as delegated by the CEO or his/her designated alternate.  The
interest/fees/commission and charges are subject to vary depending upon the loan products and
the prevailing market rates, subject to remaining with bank’s internal policies and prevailing
NRB directives.

### CHAPTER XII: RISK PARTICIPATION

##### Multiple Banking Arrangements

  - Multi banking may be required when the underlying total requirement of the client is

not within our risk appetite threshold and the Bank wishes to do business with a
borrower within a certain limit, keeping the option of easy exit open and minimizing
exposure risk to specific borrower.

   - Loose consortium means the credit facilities provided/to be provided by two or more

banks and financial institutions to a project without forming a consortium group but
maintaining security on a pari-passu basis.

   - The administrative modalities of multi banking arrangements and operations shall be

as per Nepal Rastra Bank Directives.

 ##### Consortium Arrangement

  - Extension of credit limits to borrower on consortium basis happens when two or more

than two financial institutions jointly participate in financing.  This participation of
Banks generally enables them to apply uniform standard, similar terms and conditions
and exchange of information in regard to the credit proposal.

   - The Bank could participate in consortium financing as a Lead Bank, a Joint /Co-Lead

bank or a member Bank.

   - The administrative modalities of consortium finance and operations shall be as per

Nepal Rastra Bank Directives and the Bank shall comply with the minimum provisions
of the Nepal Rastra Bank.

 ##### Credit Sale / Credit Purchase / Re-purchase & Takeover:

The bank shall make credit sale / credit purchase / re-purchase & take over, as required in
line with the NRB guidelines / internal guidelines circulated by the Bank Management.

### CHAPTER XIII: LENDING TO ENTITIES WITH
 FOREIGN INVESTMENT

The Bank shall not provide Credit Facilities to foreign nationals unless that is eligible under
Nepalese Law.

 Sanction of credit facility to entities involving foreign investment can be done based on the
credit worthiness, credibility, viability or financial guarantee of the reputed International Banks
and credibility of the holding companies and Local Investors.

 The Bank should take some caution while providing loan to entities involving Foreign
Investment in compliance with NRB provisions and national law.

 Based on comfort, the bank may sanction loan to following entities involving Foreign
Investment:

a.  **Company registered in Nepal with Foreign Direct Investment:**

Entities having Whole Ownership refers to the complete ownership/control of a
business or resource in a country by individuals who are not citizens of that country, or
by companies whose headquarters are not in that country.  The Bank shall seek
overriding comforts including credibility, ratings, reputation of such foreign investor
prior to approving any credit/ facilities to such entities.

 b.  **Joint venture between Companies registered abroad or any other foreign**

**companies and Nepal:**
A Joint Venture (JV) is a business agreement in which the parties agree to develop, for
a finite time, a new entity and new assets by contributing equity.  They exercise control
over the enterprise and consequently share revenues, expenses and assets.  The Bank
shall seek adequate comforts including credibility, ratings and reputation of such
entities as well as that of domestic investors prior to approving any credit/ facilities.

 c.  **Company registered in Nepal partially owned by foreign company, foreign**

**branches of multinational companies:**
Companies registered in Nepal may be partially owned by multinational companies.
 Also, foreign branches of multinational companies may also be established.  The Bank
shall seek adequate comforts including credibility, ratings and reputation of such
entities as well as that of domestic investors prior to approving any credit/ facilities.

 d.  **Company registered in Nepal wholly or partially owned by Non Resident Nepalese**

**Investors:**
The credit assessment of Non Resident Nepalese shall be done treating them same as
foreign investors except in case of legal privilege provided to non-resident Nepalese
and entities promoted by them.

### CHAPTER XIV: PERIODIC / ANNUAL REVIEW OF
 CREDIT LIMITS

##### Review of Individual Exposures

 - All credit exposures to a customer must generally be reviewed at least annually except

on product paper guided loans in which case the requirement of the respective product
paper should be followed.  In case of standalone term loans, review shall be conducted
as per the instruction of the management.

  - Preferably, reviews of all the accounts that are part of one Customer Group be carried

out simultaneously by the Group Relationship Manager responsible for that group,
ensuring same review date for all accounts in the group.

  - Further, regular periodic monitoring of each credit relationship to be done as demanded

by the approval terms of each Credit Limits.

  - Generally, review extensions shall not be encouraged and it should always be the

endeavour of the bank to complete the annual review well within the original expiry
date.  However, where renewal of accounts could not be completed on time due to
various reasons, review extension may be provided with approval from appropriate
authority.

 ##### Repayment Follow ups and Deviation Review/ Management

 - In addition to regular follow ups for repayment or overdue clearance, breach of other

terms and conditions of credit like document submission delay, any deferrals or failure
in commitment by the client as per offer letter and approved credit terms also to be
reviewed and managed.

  - All the concerned official should be regularly reviewing the approval

deviations/deferrals observed in such risk assets so that account is made regular as per
the approved terms and conditions and any overdue is cleared at the earliest so that
impairment charges are least to the possible extent.

 ##### Credit Portfolio Review

 - Bank shall conduct periodic credit review (product wise, sector wise, portfolio wise,

and security wise) at least on quarterly basis to keep top level management informed
regarding the current credit performance and risk concentration.

  - Product paper guided loans may be reviewed on a portfolio basis without having

required to be reviewed individually which should be mentioned clearly in the
respective product paper.

### CHAPTER V: GOOD GOVERNANCE

Financial institutions are particularly vulnerable to conflict of interest allegations given the
inherent nature of their business and their reliance on the continued confidence and goodwill
of depositors and borrowers alike.

 The Staff involved in Credit Underwriting and Approval should behave ethically in all credit
activities, declare and refrain from participating in a credit decisions involving potential
conflict of interests.  Conflict of interest, accusations against directors, officers and employees
of this Bank are to be avoided if public confidence in the Bank is to be maintained.

 Conflict of interest exists whenever directors, officers or employees benefit directly or
indirectly from the approval or operation of services given to a customer of the Bank.  Direct
benefit exists when the party in question accepts gifts in consideration of providing services
and facilities or has a direct beneficial ownership in the client company.  Indirect benefit exists
when the benefit of these transactions passes to the directors, officers or employees’ families
or business partners.  Hence, to maintain good governance in the Bank, directors, officers and
employees will not only avoid these situations but will, in so far as possible, take actions which
will avoid even the appearance of conflict of interest.  Further, NRB provisions regarding Good
Governance to be followed by all concerned during credit approval process.

### CHAPTER XVI: LOAN PROVISIONS, COLLECTION,
 RECOVERY AND WRITE OFF

##### Loan Loss Provisioning

a. The term ‘Loan Loss Provisioning’ refers to the non-cash expenses made by the Bank

to account for future losses on loan defaults.  Provisioning of loans will be done as per
the loan classification prescribed by Nepal Rastra Bank.
 b. The Bank may, at the discretion of management, set higher provisioning than that of

regulatory requirements as a prudent practice based on the risk profile of the individual
borrower, group of borrower or specific products/portfolio.

 Similarly, the Bank may reschedule and restructure the loan at the written request of the
customer along with business plan being submitted by the client, subject to the Bank being
convinced with the reason for doing so with reasonable assurance on the loan being repaid.
 Reschedule and restructure of the loan shall be done being within the broader framework as
laid down by NRB directives and provisioning to such rescheduled/ restructured accounts shall
be done as per the guidelines laid by NRB directives.

 ##### Loan Collection and Recovery

Concerned branch officials are responsible for continuous follow up for the settlement of any
due (including interest or principal) as per the terms and conditions.

 Concerned branch officials shall make rigorous follow up for settlement of overdue.  Recovery
action of classified accounts or other accounts shall be guided by the Loan Recovery Procedure
of the Bank and subsequent amendments therein.  Further, loan call back, auction notice
publishing, income recognition of default accounts etc.  shall also be as per Loan Recovery
Procedures of the Bank.

 ##### Loan Write Off 

The process and decision for writing-off of loans/advances and interest shall be guided by the
Loan Write off By-laws and Loan Recovery Procedures of the Bank.

##### 17.1 Approval and Effective Date

This Policy shall come into immediate effect upon approval by the Board of Directors.

 ##### 17.2 Repeal and Saving 

All the works performed under the previous Credit Policy/Guidelines shall be considered to
have been done under this Credit Policy.

 Any amendment in the laws/ rules/ regulations/ NRB Directives/ Circulars or any Circulars
affecting provisions under this guideline shall have automatic effect amending such provisions
under this Policy.

 In case of ambiguity in any of the matters stated in this Policy, the interpretation of the Chief
Executive Officer shall be final.

 ##### 17.3 Deviation Approval: 

Approval for deviation to any provisions under this Guideline shall rest within Board of
Directors (BOD) or as delegated by BOD.

 ##### 17.2 Repeal and Saving 

All the works performed under the previous Credit Policy/Guidelines shall be considered to
have been done under this Credit Policy.

 Any amendment in the laws/ rules/ regulations/ NRB Directives/ Circulars or any Circulars
affecting provisions under this guideline shall have automatic effect amending such provisions
under this Policy.

 In case of ambiguity in any of the matters stated in this Policy, the interpretation of the Chief
Executive Officer shall be final.

 ##### 17.3 Deviation Approval: 

Approval for deviation to any provisions under this Guideline shall rest within Board of
Directors (BOD) or as delegated by BOD.

**1. ** **Introduction**

Global IME Bank Ltd.  (GIBL) demands the highest standards of integrity and ethical conduct in its
business dealing.  The Bank will not tolerate any bribery or corrupt practices related to its business
activities from its employees or business partners.  It is committed to transparent reporting and
adopting all other reasonable measures which avoid employee's involvement in bribery or corruption.

 **2. ** **Scope**

GIBL has a vision and core values that are incompatible with bribery and corruption.  This AntiBribery & Corruption Policy applies to all Bank's activities in all jurisdictions in which it operates.
 This policy applies to all the board members and all staffs (which includes temporary as well as
contract staff) of the Bank wherever they are located.  This policy commits to conduct banking service
ethically and with the utmost integrity in all its operations throughout the world.

 The management of the Bank shall ensure that its bribery prevention policies and procedures are
understood by all staff of the Bank through internal and external communication, including training,
in proportion to the risks.

 **3. ** **Purpose**

The purpose of this Anti-Bribery and Corruption Policy is to provide Bank's staff including director,
agents, consultants and contractors as well as suppliers involved in the Bank's activities must be aware
and become familiar with a clear set of guidelines to ensure that the Bank conducts its activities in an
ethical and appropriate manner as well as complying with the laws and regulations of each jurisdiction
in which it operates.  The policy aims to:

a) Outline principles for conducting business with integrity and in accordance with the highest

ethical standards;

b) Provide guidance on the types of behavior that may give rise to violation of anti-bribery and anti
corruption laws;

c) Ensure that the financial and other resources of the Bank are used solely for proper purposes;

d) Promote a culture of honesty and openness among the Bank's staff.

 Bribery and corruption undermine the rule of law and the principle of fair competition.  The Bank’s
staff can take practical steps to mitigate the inherent risk of corrupt behaviors.  This policy aims to
inform the Bank’s staffs about Bank’s intention to closely monitor corruption risk and to take
immediate action if evidence of corrupt activity is suspected.

## 1.  Short Title& Definitions

## 1.1 Short Title and Commencement

This "Talent Hunt Guidelines" shallbe referred as "The Guideline" hereinafter.

 The contents of this guideline may be amended by the Boardas and when necessary.  This guideline (including  amendments  if  any)  shall  be  duly  communicated  to  the  concerned  staff  of  the  Bank.  Such amendments/alterations shall form an integral part of this guideline.

 Bank Management shall issue circulars/memorandums, as appropriate, to all staffs informing about "The Guideline".  All staff of the Bank must understand and be familiar with the contents of this guideline along with any amendments/alterations thereto.

 ## 1.2 Definition

Unless the subject or the context otherwise requires, in this Guideline,

- a) "The Bank" means Global IME Bank Limited.
 - b) 'The BOD' means Board of Directors.
 - c) "NRB" means Nepal Rastra Bank.
 - d) "BFIs" means a bank or financial institution which has obtained a license pursuant to Bank and Financial Institution Act 2073 BS for carrying on banking or financial transaction.
 - e) "CEO" means person appointed as the Chief Executive of the Bank, appointed by the Board and  entrusted  with  overall  Management,  Administration  and  Operations  of  the  Bank  and accountable to the Board.
 - f) "Staff" means staff of the Bank as defined in the HR By laws of the Bank.

 ## 2.  Introduction and Regulatory Requirement

## 2.1 Introduction

Human resources  are  the  most  important  resources  for  any  organization  and  this  becomes  even more important for the service industry like banking.  Experienced employees may not be available adequately  or  sometimes  experienced  employees  are  not  fulfilled  from  within  the  bank  or  from external vacancy announcement.  Hence, talent hunt is the best way to fulfill the requirement of staff in the bank whenever required.

 Talent hunt is a recruitment strategy of hiring best talents who are right fit for right type of job.  Talent hunt enables the bank to hire experienced candidates from the sources other than promotion, internal vacancy announcement and external vacancy announcement.

 ## 2.2 Regulatory Requirement

The Talent HuntGuideline has been developed in accordance with Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) Unified Directive No.  6.

 The contents of this guideline may be amended by the Boardas and when necessary.  This guideline (including  amendments  if  any)  shall  be  duly  communicated  to  the  concerned  staff  of  the  Bank.  Such amendments/alterations shall form an integral part of this guideline.

## 3.  Objective and Guiding Principles

## 3.1 Objectives of the guideline

Following are the key objectives of this guideline:

- a) To establish and enforce a transparent talent hunt practice.
 - b) To avoid confusion and ambiguity in recruitment of candidates under talent hunt and vacancy announcement.
 - c) To ensure availability of experienced manpower at all areas of the bank as and when necessary.
 - d) To fulfill suitable manpower in the bank in timely and cost effective manner.
 - e) To  fulfill the manpower  requirement created due to establishment of new  branches/ departments/subsidiaries as well as due to staff transfer and resignation.

 ## 3.2 Guiding Principles of the guideline

All Talent Hunt decisions shall be guided by following principles:

- a) Bank's need and requirement shall be the top priority in any talent hunt decision.
 - b) Recruitment under Talent Hunt shall be done within approved staff quota (Darbandi).
 - c) In general, the mode  of  selection  of candidates  shall be Interview.  However,  written examination, Group Discussion or any other practical examination, whenever required, can also be conducted while selecting candidates.
 - d) In order to fulfill the vacant positions, some candidates who were not selected previously need to be recalled for the second time.  Talent Hunt candidates can be recalled for selection process only after 2 months from the last interview date.
 - e) In order to appoint some candidates in certain positions, the remuneration of the bank may not be sufficient to them.  Hence, remuneration and facilities can be negotiated to compensate the Talent  Hunt  Candidates.   In  order  to  compensate  the  Talent  Hunt  Candidates,  the  Interview Panel can recommend additional grades and the same needs to be approved by Recruitment and Promotion Committee.
 - f) While appointing a candidate in certain position, he/she must fulfill minimum criteria as stated in  KarmachariSewaBiniyamawali,  2077  of  the  bank.   In  addition,  the  candidate  must  have minimum experience as mentioned in PPG in immediate lower position.
 - g) Talent  Hunt  shall  be  done  in  all  job  positions  except  in  Support  Level  Position,  Trainee Assistant and Management Trainee Positions.  However, in cases where requirement of Trainee Assistants  and  Management  Trainees  needs  to  be  fulfilled  via  College  Placement,  the recruitment can be considered under Talent Hunt.
 - h) For  any  issue  that  is  not  covered  herein,  the  talent  hunt  decisions  shall  be  guided  by KarmachariSewaBiniyamawali, 2077 of the bank.

## 1.  Correspondent Banking Definition

Correspondent Banking relationships are commonly used by banks internationally to undertake  financial  transactions  for  themselves  and  their  customers  in  jurisdictions where they generally have no physical presence.  A wide range of services can be settled through a correspondent banking relationship, including:

- a) Payments, including electronic transfers, drafts etc.
 - b) Buy / Sell of foreign exchanges
- c) Collections
- d) Placement of funds
- e) Trade finance transactions
- f) Counter Guarantees
- g) Remittances

Correspondent Banking relationships are established in two forms.  Other Banks and Financial Institutions (BFIs) may establish relationship with us (Vostro Account) and we may also need to establish relationship with local and international Banks (Nostro Account).

## 2.  Risks in Correspondent Banking

- 2.1 Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing: Correspondent banking relationships are exposed to money laundering and terrorism financing because they involve a bank carrying out financial transactions on behalf of another bank's customers.  On such indirect relationship we should depend on correspondent banks where our bank cannot verify the identities and obtain first-hand information about those customers.   If they do not undertake an appropriate level of initial and ongoing due diligence on such accounts, our  Bank may be exposed to risks associated with money laundering or terrorism financing.  'Layering' is a major risk the bank is exposed to and the Bank must be careful while selecting correspondent banking relationship.  It is the process by  depositing  money  in  one  bank  and  transferring  it  to  another  bank  in  the  same country or other country to convert the fund earned from illegal source to legal source.
 - 2.2 Reputational  Risk: Bank  has  a  risk  of  losing  its  reputation  by  unknowingly transacting funds originated from illegal activities if its correspondent bank fails to implement adequate or appropriate measures to prevent Money laundering or Terrorist Financing.
 - 2.3 Financial  Risk: Financially  weak  performance,  operational  failure  or  any  other unexpected event can cause bankruptcy of a correspondent bank which consequently results into financial loss to banks maintaining nostro account relation.
 - 2.4 Business  Risk: Correspondent  bank's  failure  to  execute  or  timely  execute  any transactions on behalf of the bank can hamper business or can cause financial/reputational loss to the bank.  Therefore, while choosing correspondent bank consideration of business reliability becomes very important.

 - 2.5 Country Risk: This risk may arise while maintaining fund in nostro account in the foreign country.  Massive changes in political system, change in regulated exchange rate  can  have  adverse  effects  on  business  of  a  correspondent  Bank.   Similarly, correspondent relationship is vulnerable to sovereign risk and transfer risk, which is the risk of capital being locked up or frozen by the government action.

## Mitigation and Measures

- a) Bank shall not establish any type (Nostro, Vostro or Relationship Management-RMA) of correspondent relationship with:
- i. Banks not having physical presence in any country (Shell bank) and any banks which carried out transactions with shell banks.
 - ii.  Unlicensed and/or unregulated financial institutions.
 - iii.  Any financial Institution and the country restricted by Nepal Rastra Bank or Government of Nepal or United Nations or any other internationally recognized authorities or local regulatory authority.
 - b) The  following  requirements  are  set  forth  for  establishing  Nostro  account relationship  and  Relationship  Management  (RMA)  with  any  banks  outside Nepal:
- i. Bank must have positive net worth to enter into correspondent relationship with Global IME Bank Ltd.
 - ii.  The bank should not be subject to sanctions, embargoes or similar measures issued  by  Nepal  or  United  Nations  or  FATF  or  any  other  internationally recognized authorities or local regulatory authority.
 - iii.  Correspondent Bank and International Bank must have minimum equivalent rating of B3/B- by any of renowned rating agency(ies), like Moody, Standard & Poor, and Fitch, etc.  In case of correspondent bank in India and other SAARC countries, local rating agencies may also be considered.  Localized ratings or implied ratings on Bloomberg/Reuters portal are also acceptable as long as they are similar or higher than B3/B- as mentioned above.  Banks appearing in the top 1000, Bankers' publications are also acceptable.
 - iv.  The maintenance of Nostro account relationship with any correspondent bank is subject to written approval from Nepal Rastra Bank which will be sufficient for the purpose of Due Diligence and documentation requirement.  ALCO shall set/review  the  credit  limit/ceiling  in  such  accounts.   A  credit  assessment  for Nostro Relationship is required and such is to be performed by the ALCO based on Treasury Department's recommendations.
 - v. Foreign Banks not meeting any one of the above criteria will be disqualified for establishing Nostro account relationship and Relationship Management (RMA).

- a) Bank shall not establish any type (Nostro, Vostro or Relationship Management-RMA) of correspondent relationship with:
- i. Banks not having physical presence in any country (Shell bank) and any banks which carried out transactions with shell banks.

metadata.author: Shishir Shakya

- c) The following requirements set forth for establishing vostro account relationship by any BFIs  outside or inside Nepal:
- i. Relationship  shall  be  established  with  the  BFIs  which  are  monitored  and supervised  by  the  regulatory  authority  with  respect  to  AML  and  Terrorist financing.
 - ii.  BFI's should have Anti Money Laundering (AML) policy.
 - iii.  Country of the Correspondent bank should have appropriate AML laws and regulations.
 - iv.  The bank should not be subject to sanctions, embargoes or similar measures issued  by  Nepal  or  United  Nations  or  FATF  or  any  other  internationally recognized authorities or local regulatory authority.
 - v. To establish or continue relationship with a bank from a nation which does not follow  international  practices  and  norms  relating  to  AML  and  terrorist financing, detailed due diligence evaluation is to be carried out.   In such cases, background  of  owner/beneficiary  of  correspondent  bank  and  its  policy  and strategy for prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing are to be examined thoroughly.
 - vi.  Bank  shall  obtain  the  following  information  about  the  correspondent  bank before establishing a relationship:
- (a) Profile of Executive Management
- (b) Location of Major Business units/ activities
- (c) Prevention effort made on AML and anti-terrorist financing
- (d) Regulator
- (e) System of regulation and monitoring of home country of correspondent bank
- (f) Purpose of account (in case of vostro relationship)
- vii.  Required documents from Financial Institutions shall be as per the Directive/Circular  of  NRB/FIU  and  KYC  manual  of  the  bank.   Without impairing the generality prescribed by them, the following shall be the other required documents:
- (a) Response to AML questionnaire (as set by our Compliance Department)
- (b) Updated  copy  of  Corporate  Anti-Money  Laundering  Policies  and/or Procedures
- (c) Brief profile of Board Members and Senior Management
- (d) Latest Annual Report
- (e) Signature Booklet
- viii.  Any  deviation  on  the  response  to  AML  questionnaire  from  the  expected response shall require approval from compliance officer of the bank.

## 3.  Responsibility

Treasury  Department,  which  is  currently  looking  after  Correspondent  Banking  shall ensure that proposed financial institution meets all the criteria set forth by the policy and obtain all the necessary documents before establishing correspondent relationships for Nostro account.  The department is also entrusted with the responsibility to update the information  on  periodic basis and  monitor  and  manage  relationships  with  the correspondent banks.

 ## 4.  Compliance/Audit

Compliance and Audit Department will have the responsibility of reviewing correspondent  banking  documents  and  processes  on  periodic  basis  to  ensure  the fulfillment of the requirement sent forth by the policy.

 ## 5.  Miscellaneous

- i. This policy shall be reviewed whenever it is deemed necessary.
 - ii.  This policy, and amendment thereto, shall come into effect from the date of approval by the Board of Directors of the Bank.
